theory.intro: Once a variable is numerical or categorical, it has a **subtype**. A numerical variable is **discrete** or **continuous**. A categorical variable is **nominal** or **ordinal**.
facts: **Discrete** numerical values come from **counting** and jump in whole steps, such as goals scored or seats on a bus.
**Continuous** numerical values come from **measuring** and can be any value in a range, such as height, time or mass.
**Nominal** categories have no natural order, such as eye colour, suburb or brand of car.
**Ordinal** categories have a natural order, such as clothing size, report grade or level of satisfaction.
Careful: sizes like small, medium and large are **ordinal**, not nominal, because they have an order.
A count stays **discrete** even when the numbers are very large, such as the size of a crowd.

foundation.question_text:
The variable **number of sheep in Australia** is numerical.
Is it discrete or continuous?

The variable **time taken to complete a test** is numerical.
Is it discrete or continuous?
foundation.solution_text:
Time is **measured** and can take any value in a range.
**Continuous.**

foundation.question_text:
The variable **number of students late to school today** is numerical.
Is it discrete or continuous?

The variable **mass of a schoolbag** is numerical.
Is it discrete or continuous?
foundation.solution_text:
Mass is **measured** and can take any value in a range.
**Continuous.**

foundation.question_text:
The variable **method of travel to work** is categorical.
Is it nominal or ordinal?
foundation.solution_text:
Travel methods (car, bus, walk) have **no natural order**.
**Nominal.**

foundation.question_text:
The variable **report grade from A to E** is categorical.
Is it nominal or ordinal?
foundation.solution_text:
Grades have a **natural order** from A to E.
**Ordinal.**

development.question_text:
The variable **suburb of home** is categorical.
Is it nominal or ordinal?

The variable **level of satisfaction with the government** is categorical.
Is it nominal or ordinal?
development.solution_text:
Satisfaction levels run from low to high, so they have a **natural order**.
**Ordinal.**

development.question_text:
The variable **school population** is numerical.
Is it discrete or continuous?

The variable **height of a Year 9 student** is numerical.
Is it discrete or continuous?
development.solution_text:
Height is **measured** and can take any value in a range.
**Continuous.**

mastery.question_text:
The variable **clothing size (small, medium, large)** is categorical.
A student says it is nominal because the sizes are just names.
Is it nominal or ordinal?
mastery.solution_text:
Small, medium and large follow a **natural order** from smallest to largest.
Because the categories can be ordered, the variable is **ordinal**, not nominal.

mastery.question_text:
The variable **number of people at a concert** is numerical.
Because the number is very large, a student says it is continuous.
Is it discrete or continuous?
mastery.solution_text:
The people are **counted** in whole steps — you cannot have half a person.
A large count is still counted, so the variable is **discrete**, not continuous.

mastery.question_text:
Zach classifies **age** as discrete; Ed classifies it as continuous.
Explain how each could be correct.
mastery.solution_text:
If age is recorded as a whole number of years (a count), it is **discrete**.
If age is measured exactly — to the day, hour or second — it can take any value, so it is **continuous**.
Both are correct, depending on how age is recorded.
